newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Drift into industry.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Drift into industry.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV political Correspondent)
"No major company can afford to ignore the realities of its marketplace." -- Industry Minister John Moore, April 29.
Nor can any government.

And Moore's rather blase reaction to BHP's decison to end steelmaking in Newcastle and retrench 2,500 workers may have marked the beginning of the end of the Howard government's romance with free-market rhetoric.
However, a shift to a coherent industry policy is still not on the horizon -- despite the increasing shrill clarion calls from business.
Moore is a mercurial man of many parts -- able to mouth quite contradictory policy positions without the slightest blush.
Just as he was giving BHP the government's blessing on the grounds of "competitiveness", he was doing his darndest to make sure more competition was not visited on the car industry.
It worked, too, and, paradoxically, one significant reason was the Howard government's laissez-faire reaction to the BHP decision.

As serendipity would have it, at the time of the Newcastle announcement, respected pollster Rod Cameron was in the midst of polling commissioned by the Minerals Council about public attitudes to industry policy.
On BHP, he reported that: "Perhaps no single announcement by a company in recent years has had a greater unsettling impact on ordinary Australians than this one has."

When Australians are anything but "relaxed and comfortable" the image of the Big Australian downsizing can only increase the paranoia of mainstream Australia about job security at the top of the voters' list of concerns.
It was a volatile mixture -- and a powerful argument in the hands of the protectionist forces arrayed against cuts in car tariffs.
South Australia's John Olsen, for example, reminded John Howard of the displacement costs should the Mitsubishi plant in his state be forced out of business and its workforce retrenched.
Not to mention the impact it would have had on the South Austalian premier's re-election chances. In the end, the momentum to water down the tariff cuts was irresistable.
It was a big loss for Treasurer Peter Costello.
The fact that the decision did nothing at all to test the car makers brought all the other protectionists out of the shrubbery.

National party backwoodsmen like Bob Katter and De-Anne Kelly -- playing to the cheap seats -- immediately demanded sugar tariffs be maintained even though the industry had pushed for their abolition and even though 85 percent of production -- and rising -- is destined for the overseas market.
Just as quick out of the blocks was the textile, clothing and footwear (TCF) industry, even before the Productivity Commission's report on its tariffs -- expected out next week -- hits the deck.
That could prove even hotter for the government to handle.
Many TCF concerns are concentrated in marginal electorates -- just where the government's welcome is wearing thinnest.

It's interesting, though, that some of the younger and smarter apparel manufacturers noted that the TCF tariff serves only to discourage productivity gains and makes it harder for them to compete overseas where the real money stands to be made.

The car tariff decision will almost certainly guarantee Olsen's re-election, but as the instant reaction from other protectionists shows the downstream effect on the federal government will be all on the downside.
As events have already shown it makes it just that much harder for Howard to argue credibly against the sectional interests lining up for their bucket of money from the government.
To make matters worse, this has come as employment heads south again despite the series of interest rate cuts over the past 12 months.
No one predicted a fall as big as 40,000 in the employment number issued on Thursday.

The market reaction was instant, factoring in market rhetoric, too. For example, Bill Shields from Macquarie Bank declared that the jobless figures "...marked a bigger problem than just a lack of demand in the economy. It could not be addressed, he declared "simply ...by cutting interest rates..."

The government's initial response was to have Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone declare that the policy settings were right, that they would take time to work, that the policy of "spend, spend, spend" had failed and it was not the time for instant "Nescafe" solutions.
Well, that should do the trick.
Not with Howard's increasingly nervous backbench it won't.
And the prime minister's cave in to the car industry will only make it harder for him to argue credibly against more government intervention, more government spending.
And as the prime minister said from opposition that won't create "real jobs" either.
-- Canberra bureau 61-6 273-2730
